titulo_es: The future in the past (was going to, was to, was about to, would)
descripcion_es: Talking from a past point of view about something that was then in the future: was going to, was to, was about to, would, was due to.
resumen: To narrate what, at a moment in the past, was still to come, English puts its future forms into the past. Each one keeps its nuance: intention, official plan, imminence or a destiny known with hindsight.

filas: was / were going to + inf.
Intention or prediction, often not fulfilled
I was going to call you, but I forgot.
would + inf.
Future seen from the past (reported speech, narrative)
She knew he would be late.
was / were to + inf.
Official plan or arrangement
The minister was to open the new hospital.
was / were to have + past participle
Plan that did not happen
The wedding was to have taken place in May.
was / were about to + inf.
Imminence (be on the verge of)
We were about to leave when it started to rain.
was / were on the point of + -ing
Imminence, more emphatic
He was on the point of giving up.
was / were due to + inf.
Timetable or scheduled date
The train was due to arrive at six.
was / were + -ing
Plan already arranged
I was meeting Sue that evening, so I couldn't stay.

explicacion.texto: Was to + infinitive also has a narrative use of “destiny”: what, as we now know, was going to happen later. It is equivalent to Spanish “estaba destinado a” or “llegaría a”: He left school at fifteen; he was never to return.

items: Was going to often suggests that the plan did not happen: I was going to buy it, but it was sold out.
Was about to is not combined with specific time expressions: not “was about to leave at five”.
Would is the usual form in reported speech: He said he would help (Spanish “dijo que ayudaría”).

ejemplos.frase: I was going to paint the kitchen, but I ran out of time.
ejemplos.traduccion: Iba a pintar la cocina, pero me quedé sin tiempo.

ejemplos.frase: Little did she know that she would become the company's first female director.
ejemplos.traduccion: Poco sabía ella que llegaría a ser la primera directora de la empresa.

ejemplos.frase: The two leaders were to meet in Geneva the following week.
ejemplos.traduccion: Los dos dirigentes debían reunirse en Ginebra la semana siguiente.

ejemplos.frase: The bridge was to have been finished by 2020.
ejemplos.traduccion: El puente tendría que haberse terminado en 2020.

ejemplos.frase: I was just about to send the email when the power went off.
ejemplos.traduccion: Estaba a punto de enviar el correo cuando se fue la luz.

ejemplos.frase: They said goodbye at the station; they were never to see each other again.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se despidieron en la estación; no volverían a verse nunca.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I knew she will be angry.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I knew she would be angry.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: From a point in the past, the future is expressed with would.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I was going to call you but I have forgotten.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The narrative continues in the past simple.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: We were about to leaving when he arrived.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: We were about to leave when he arrived.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Be about to takes an infinitive; on the point of takes -ing.

ejercicios.frase: I ___ tell you the news, but you had already heard it.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was going to + infinitive expresses a past intention and, as the rules and key points say, it often suggests that the plan did not happen. The clue is the but that follows: you had already heard it, so the intention was frustrated. That is why the form is was going to, the exact equivalent of Spanish “iba a” in this context.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A past intention that was not carried out: was going to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Iba a contarte la noticia, pero ya te habías enterado.

por_opcion.was going to: Correct: a past intention that was not carried out.
por_opcion.will: Incorrect: will looks at the future from the present; it does not fit in a past narrative.
por_opcion.am about to: Incorrect: it is in the present and expresses present imminence, not a past intention.
por_opcion.would have: Incorrect: would have + past participle is the past conditional; also, here it would be followed by tell, not told, and it would change the meaning.

ejercicios.frase: The film was just ___ start when the fire alarm went off.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was/were about to + infinitive expresses imminence, “be on the verge of”. The clues are just, which emphasises how close it was, the infinitive start after the gap and the structure when + past simple, which introduces the interruption. The form is about to, which is followed by the infinitive with no extra to.
ejercicios.traduccion: La película estaba a punto de empezar cuando sonó la alarma de incendios.

por_opcion.about to: Correct: was just about to start, imminence in the past.
por_opcion.going: Incorrect: “was just going start” is missing to; was going to would be possible, but this option is incomplete.
por_opcion.due: Incorrect: due needs to (was due to start) and expresses a scheduled time, not imminence.
por_opcion.on the point of: Incorrect: on the point of is followed by -ing (on the point of starting), not by an infinitive.

ejercicios.frase: The concert ___ have taken place last night, but it was cancelled.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was/were to have + past participle expresses an official plan that did not happen. The clues are have taken place, which requires a structure with have + past participle, and but it was cancelled, which confirms that the plan failed. Also, a scheduled concert is an arrangement or official plan, the typical context for was to. The answer is was to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: An official plan that did not happen: was to have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: El concierto tenía que haberse celebrado anoche, pero se canceló.

por_opcion.will: Incorrect: will have taken place is the future perfect and does not fit with last night or with a cancelled plan.
por_opcion.was to: Correct: was to have + past participle, a planned event that did not take place.
por_opcion.was about to: Incorrect: about to takes a simple infinitive and expresses imminence, not a frustrated official plan.
por_opcion.is to: Incorrect: it is in the present and cannot be combined with last night.

ejercicios.frase: She promised that she ___ write every week.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table and in the rules and key points: would is the usual future form in reported speech. The clue is the reporting verb in the past, promised: from that past moment, the writing was in the future, so will becomes would. It is exactly the change from Spanish “escribirá” to “escribiría” when reporting what someone said.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Reported speech in the past: will becomes would.
ejercicios.traduccion: Prometió que escribiría todas las semanas.

por_opcion.will: Incorrect: after a reporting verb in the past, will becomes would (a typical mistake listed on the card).
por_opcion.would: Correct: the future seen from the past in reported speech.
por_opcion.is going to: Incorrect: it is in the present; at most it would be was going to.
por_opcion.was about to: Incorrect: it expresses imminence and does not fit with a promise about every week.

ejercicios.frase: The plane was ___ to land at 10.15, but it was delayed.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table about be due to: a time expected according to a timetable. The clue is the exact time 10.15, typical of a flight timetable, and the to that already appears after the gap. The word the card practises is due: was due to land. was supposed to, was expected to and was scheduled to are also accepted, as they express the same unfulfilled expectation. The later but shows that the timetable was not kept.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Be due to: time expected according to a timetable (supposed, expected or scheduled are also valid).
ejercicios.traduccion: El avión tenía prevista la llegada a las 10.15, pero se retrasó.

errores_previstos.respuesta: about
errores_previstos.explicacion: About to expresses imminence and, as the rules and key points warn, it is not combined with a specific time; for a timetable, use due to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: due to
errores_previstos.explicacion: The to is already written after the gap; if you add it, the sentence has to twice (was due to to land). Only due is missing.

ejercicios.frase: He emigrated in 1950. He ___ never to see his homeland again.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the narrative use of was to + infinitive explained on the card: “destiny”, what, as we now know, was going to happen later. The clue is never to see, which shows the structure was never to + infinitive, and the biographical context. The word is was. Spanish expresses it with the conditional (“nunca volvería a ver”) or with “estaba destinado a”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Was to with the meaning of destiny: “he would never see again”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Emigró en 1950. Nunca volvería a ver su tierra natal.

errores_previstos.respuesta: would
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would is not followed by to (would never see); the structure with to is was never to see.

errores_previstos.respuesta: is
errores_previstos.explicacion: The story is in the past; destiny seen from the past is was to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: had
errores_previstos.explicacion: Had never to see does not have that meaning; the form for destiny is was to.

glosario.definicion_l: the country where you were born

ejercicios.frase: I was on the point ___ resigning when they offered me a promotion.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was/were on the point of + -ing expresses imminence, more emphatically than about to. The clue is on the point followed by resigning in -ing. The missing word is the preposition of, which completes the fixed expression. As the card reminds you, about to takes an infinitive and on the point of takes -ing.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Be on the point of + -ing: be about to do something.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estaba a punto de dimitir cuando me ofrecieron un ascenso.

errores_previstos.respuesta: to
errores_previstos.explicacion: It copies Spanish “a punto de”; the expression is on the point of, which is why it is followed by -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: for
errores_previstos.explicacion: The preposition in the expression is of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: about
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes two structures: about to or on the point of, but not “on the point about”.

glosario.definicion_l: a message issued in behalf of some product or cause or idea or person or institution · act of raising in rank or position

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form.
ejercicios.frase: I couldn't come to dinner because I ___ (meet) a client that evening.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the idea on the card that future forms are put into the past while keeping their nuance: the present continuous for arrangements becomes the past continuous. The clue is that evening and the excuse of an appointment already arranged at that time. That is why was meeting is valid; was going to meet is also accepted, presenting the appointment as an intention already decided.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Past continuous for a plan already arranged in the past.
ejercicios.traduccion: No pude ir a cenar porque esa tarde había quedado con un cliente.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will meet
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will looks at the future from today; a past narrative needs a past form.

errores_previstos.respuesta: met
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past simple presents the meeting as something that happened, not as a plan that prevented going to dinner.

errores_previstos.respuesta: am meeting
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present continuous does not fit in a past narrative; use was meeting.

ejercicios.frase: She said she will phone me later, but she never did.
respuestas: She said she would phone me later, but she never did.
She said she'd phone me later, but she never did.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the point in the rules and key points: would is the usual future form in reported speech. The clue is said, a reporting verb in the past, and but she never did, which confirms that the promise is no longer valid. That is why will must become would (or the contraction she'd). It is the typical mistake listed on the card.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: As the promise is no longer valid, the future in the past is would.
ejercicios.traduccion: Dijo que me llamaría más tarde, pero nunca lo hizo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She said she will phone me later, but she never did.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: after said, and with the promise already in the past, will becomes would.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She said she would phone me later, but she never would.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It also changes the ending; the second part narrates a fact and is in the past simple with did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She said she was phoning me later, but she never did.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past continuous would express an arranged appointment, not a promise; the reported-speech form is would.

ejercicios.frase: We were about to going out when the phone rang.
respuestas: We were about to go out when the phone rang.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: be about to + infinitive expresses imminence, and the card lists adding -ing as a typical mistake. The clue is about to followed by going: the to in about to is the infinitive marker, not a preposition, so it requires the base form go. The correction is were about to go out.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estábamos a punto de salir cuando sonó el teléfono.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We were about to going out when the phone rang.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: after about to comes the infinitive without -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We were about going out when the phone rang.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It removes to; the expression is about to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We were on the point to go out when the phone rang.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes structures: on the point of + -ing, or about to + infinitive.

ejercicios.frase: I intended to buy a new laptop, but I changed my mind.
respuestas: I was going to buy a new laptop, but I changed my mind.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the point in the rules and key points: was going to often suggests that the plan did not happen. The clue is intended to (“had the intention of”) and but I changed my mind. Replace I intended to buy with I was going to buy, keeping the rest. The form of be agrees with I: was.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A frustrated past intention: was going to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Iba a comprarme un portátil nuevo, pero cambié de opinión.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was going to bought a new laptop, but I changed my mind.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After going to comes the infinitive: buy, not the past form bought.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I am going to buy a new laptop, but I changed my mind.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is in the present; a past intention requires was going to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was going to buy a new laptop, but I have changed my mind.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The narrative continues in the past simple, as the card points out: I changed my mind.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite using “was about to” and remove “at any moment”, which is no longer needed.
ejercicios.frase: The ship was going to sink at any moment.
respuestas: The ship was about to sink.
The ship was just about to sink.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was about to + infinitive for imminence in the past. The clue is at any moment in the original sentence, which shows that the sinking was imminent. When you use was about to, at any moment disappears because the structure itself already expresses that imminence; it can be reinforced with just (was just about to sink).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Imminence in the past: was about to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: El barco estaba a punto de hundirse.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The ship was about to sinking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After about to comes the infinitive, not -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The ship was about sink.
errores_previstos.explicacion: to is missing: the expression is about to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The ship is about to sink.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is in the present; the original sentence is about the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The ship was about to sink at any moment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It keeps at any moment, which repeats the idea of imminence that was about to already gives; the instruction asks you to remove it.

respuestas: The president was to visit the region in June
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: was/were to + infinitive expresses an official plan or arrangement in the past. The clue is the subject The president and the official visit to a region, a typical context of an institutional agenda. The order is subject + was to + infinitive + complements: The president was to visit the region in June.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Official plan in the past: was to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estaba previsto que el presidente visitara la región en junio.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The president to visit was the region in June
errores_previstos.explicacion: It separates was from to visit; the fixed structure is was to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Was the president to visit the region in June
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is a question or an inverted conditional, not the statement required.

respuestas: We knew it would be difficult
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: would + infinitive expresses the future seen from the past, in reported speech or narrative. The clue is knew, a verb in the past: from that moment, the difficulty was in the future, so would be is used. The order is subject + knew + it + would + be + difficult. It is the same case as the typical mistake on the card, I knew she will be angry.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Future seen from the past: would + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We knew would it be difficult
errores_previstos.explicacion: It inverts as in a question; in reported speech the order is subject + verb: it would be.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We would knew it be difficult
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes up the verbs: would goes with be, and knew is the main verb.

descripcion_larga_es: When we narrate the past, we often need to talk about what was still to come at that time: what someone was going to do, what was planned or what was about to happen. English puts its future forms into the past (was going to, would, was to, was about to), and each one keeps its nuance. Spanish speakers find it hard to choose between them because Spanish handles almost everything with “iba a” or the conditional.

contexto.que_es: It is the set of forms that express a future seen from a moment in the past: was/were going to, would, was/were to (and was to have + past participle), was/were about to, was/were on the point of + -ing, was/were due to and the past continuous for plans. They are equivalent to Spanish “iba a”, “haría”, “estaba previsto que”, “estaba a punto de”.
contexto.por_que_importa: They are essential for narrating, reporting what someone said (reported speech) and explaining plans that did not happen, which is very common in reports, news and historical presentations. Choosing the wrong one changes the nuance: a frustrated intention (was going to) is not the same as an official plan (was to) or something imminent (was about to). A will where would was needed is one of the most noticeable mistakes in an exam.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It appears in narratives, in reported speech after said, promised or knew, and when explaining cancelled plans (but…). The signals are a reporting verb in the past, a but announcing that the plan failed, expressions such as just or when + past for imminence, and official contexts for was to. Spanish speakers tend to keep will after a past verb or to add -ing after about to.
